newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: golf-Hislop sounds warning with big golf win.
newsitem.headline: golf-Hislop sounds warning with big golf win.

text.p: CHRISTCHURCH, April 18 - New Zealand international Richard Hislop sounded a clear warning to the rest of the field when he ended Richard Best's bid for a slice of history at the national amateur golf championships on Thursday, NZPA reports.
Best, from Palmerston North, was aiming to become the first golfer to ever win the North Island, South Island and New Zealand amateur titles in one year.
Instead the 21-year-old Kiwi representative found himself bundled out in the first round of matchplay 5 and 4 by Hislop, despite only shooting one bogey in 14 holes.
Hislop was unstoppable, firing four birdies in a bogey-free round. His only blemish was a drive deep into trees at the sixth, where he neatly extricated himself and still made par to halve the hole.

The 23-year-old Wellingtonian had signalled his good form with a strong strokeplay challenge, which only stalled in Wednesday's rain when he elected to preserve his position in the top 32 rather than charge the leaders and risk falling apart in the soggy conditions.
Now, with an impressive early scalp to his name, Hislop is feeling primed to push on in the championship race.
"All aspects of my game are strong at the moment, so I've got no major concerns," he said.

"I'll stick to my game-plan, which I think is crucial here because there some tricky little driving holes and if you can thread the needle between the trees on four or five holes, the others will fall into place."

That's certainly what Hislop did yesterday, driving straight and hitting his irons close to the pin to set up a score that would have challenged Martin Pettigrew's course record three-under 68 had it run the distance.
"Really I just didn't make a mistake and when I got to two or three up, it put the pressure on Richie and he wasn't quite on his game," he said.
Best, who flies out for a major Argentine tournament with Hislop on Monday, said he had been on the back foot from the start and powerless to get back into the match.
"I played pretty average today and Richard was playing so well I never had a chance to get back into it," he said.
Pettigrew, meanwhile, saw his pessimism return to haunt him as he crashed out of the championship.

Thorburn, beaten by Pettigrew at the same stage last year, admitted he had "got out of jail" when his opponent lost the 18th after his drive finished in a fairway divot and he could only squirt the ball out into rough and take bogey.
Pettigrew conceded he had let Thorburn off the hook with some tentative putting before his bad luck at the 18th.
"If I had putted half decently, I would have won," he said. "I gave myself lots of opportunities but my short game was atrocious."
On Wednesday the Wellingtonian was crowned national strokeplay champion but afterwards warned that the title would count for little during the hunt for the national amateur champion.

Less than 24 hours later that thought became fact as he lost at the 19th hole to a birdie from Aucklander Tim Thorburn, the bottom-ranked qualifier who had only got into the field with a sudden-death win the night before; ironically with a birdie at the same hole.

However Pettigrew was not the only top strokeplayer to struggle during yesterday's matchplay, with runner-up Andrew Hobbs (Windsor) bundled out 2 and 1 by Queenslander Andrew Suosaari who, like Thorburn, only qualified via sudden-death.

Carterton international Reon Sayer was 2-up after five holes against Titirangi's Logan Scott but in the end needed 21 holes to secure victory, which came after Scott missed a winning birdie from 2m at the 20th.
Motueka's Hadyn Morgan, another New Zealand rep, fired a 7m birdie at the 18th to pip fellow international Steve Gordon of Redwood Park. He takes on Thorburn in tomorrow morning's second round.
